doc.title: Vince Giordano interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

title: Playing along with records and joining the union
summary: At about 12 he tried playing tuba along with his records, then sought out live music on Long Island and joined the union.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: No. No. They would come over and — “don’t play that stuff, don’t play that stuff.” They couldn’t understand me for anything. That’s fine. I chose the other path as the poet said. The one fateful day that really got me thinking about pursuing a career in this music was I was playing one of my old recordings and I had my tuba home, and I listened to it and I decided to try to play along with the recording. And I was maybe 12 years old. I could feel the beat but I really didn’t have enough musicality to understand chord changes and I was just a beginner. I would kind of sync up but not really know what to do. And that magic moment was the time when I said I want to do something with this older music today in my generation. And that’s when I started to seek out a place out on Long Island that had a live music policy, particularly older music that I could study, early popular music of the twenties and sometimes some jazz involved, and just basically get into the professional music world. I joined the union, I schlepped a tuba and later a string bass up two flights of stairs after the union fellow says, “why did you bring all this here? Did you bring your money?” That’s all he wanted. He didn’t care if I could play or not.

I’ve heard variations on that story. That’s so funny. Derek Smith, the piano player, they took him in a room and they said, “what is that?” He said, “what do you mean?” He says, “what is that?” He says, “it’s a piano.” He says, “you’re in.”
Exactly. Oh it was some wild times.
